decks.title: Ledger — Part 1: Posting from the Journal, Balancing and Reading Balances
goals: State the meaning, importance and format of the ledger, including the running balance form, and the use of the ledger folio and the journal folio
Post journal entries, simple, compound and opening entries, to ledger accounts using To and By and naming the other account
Balance real and personal accounts with balance c/d and balance b/d and read a debit or credit balance correctly

slides.heading: Ledger: posting and balancing
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the **ledger** is, its **format and folios**, **posting** from the journal, and **balancing** real and personal accounts.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: a transaction is recorded in the journal, posted to the ledger accounts and then each account is balanced
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on the ledger. The journal records each transaction in date order, but a trader also wants to know how much cash is in hand, how much a customer owes and how much a supplier is owed. The ledger gives every item an account of its own. In this part we post, balance and read accounts, using an imagined coir works.

slides.heading: The ledger: meaning and importance
bullets: The **ledger** is the principal book of accounts: it has a separate account for each person, asset, liability, expense and income.
It is written up from the **journal**, so it is a book of secondary entry.
It brings together everything about one account, so its **balance** is found at once.

rows: First book: transactions are entered here first
Second book: written up from the journal
Both accounts of a transaction together, with narration
The effect on one account at a time, no narration
Ledger folio (L.F.): page of the account in the ledger
Journal folio (J.F.): page of the journal
Shows the balance of every account

visual.alt: Table comparing the journal and the ledger on stage, order, entry, folio column and result

slides.narration: The ledger is the principal book of accounts. After a transaction is recorded in the journal, its effect is carried to the ledger account of each item involved. The journal shows what happened in date order. The ledger shows, account by account, where the firm stands. That is why the balance of cash, of a debtor or of a creditor is read from the ledger and not from the journal.

slides.heading: Format of a ledger account
slides.body_md: In the **T-form** the page has two sides. The left is the **debit** side and the right is the **credit** side. Each side has date, particulars, journal folio and amount.

visual.alt: Two sided ledger account of Parvati Coir Works, an imagined firm: the debit side with date, particulars, journal folio and amount on the left and the same four columns for the credit side on the right, with To on the debit side and By on the credit side
visual.caption: Cash A/c of an imagined firm in T-form (first lines only)

slides.narration: A ledger account is drawn as a letter T. The left side is the debit side and the right side is the credit side. Each side has four columns: date, particulars, journal folio and amount. The name of the account is written at the top. On the debit side every particular begins with the word To and on the credit side with the word By.

slides.heading: The running balance form
slides.body_md: Customer and supplier accounts are often kept in a form with a **balance column** worked out after every entry. It gives the balance at any moment but is not a T-form.

visual.alt: Running balance form of the account of Ismail and Sons: a sale of one lakh eighty thousand rupees, a receipt and a return, with the balance worked out after every line, ending at fifty thousand rupees debit
visual.caption: Ismail and Sons A/c in running balance form

slides.narration: Besides the T-form there is the running balance form. It has columns for date, particulars, folio, debit, credit and a balance that is worked out after every single entry. Banks and big firms use it for customer accounts because the balance is always visible. In this chapter, however, our main format is the two sided T-form, which is balanced only at the end of the period.

slides.heading: Folios: the link between journal and ledger
bullets: The **ledger folio** (L.F.) in the journal gives the page of the account in the ledger. It is written **after posting**.
The **journal folio** (J.F.) in the ledger gives the page of the journal from which the item was posted.

rows: *(Being the assets, the liability and the capital brought forward from the old books)*
*(Being goods bought on credit from Venkat Fibre Co.)*

visual.alt: Journal of Parvati Coir Works with a ledger folio column: the opening entry, a credit purchase and a cash sale, each account carrying the page number of its ledger account
visual.caption: The L.F. column is filled after posting

slides.narration: Two folio columns tie the books together. In the journal, the ledger folio column carries the page of each account in the ledger, filled in once the entry has been posted. In the ledger, the journal folio column carries the journal page from which the item came. With the two, any entry can be traced from either book to the other.

slides.heading: The rule of posting: To and By
bullets: Post each **debit** to the debit side of its account, writing **To** and the **other account**.
Post each **credit** to the credit side, writing **By** and the **other account**.
When two or more accounts stand on the other side, write **Sundries**.

headers: Particulars written in its ledger account
rows: Cash A/c Dr to Sales A/c (9 Apr)
Wages A/c Dr and Rent A/c Dr to Cash A/c (30 Jun)
Furniture A/c Dr to Cash A/c and Venkat Fibre Co. A/c (3 Oct)
Cash A/c and Venkat Fibre Co. A/c

visual.alt: Table of the rule of posting: the debited account carries To and the name of the other account, the credited account carries By and the name of the other account, and Sundries is written when two or more accounts stand on the other side

slides.narration: Posting follows one rule. Take the account debited in the entry, go to its page and write the amount on the debit side, with the word To and the name of the other account of the entry. For the account credited, write the amount on the credit side with the word By and the name of the other account. If the other side has more than one account, write Sundries.

slides.heading: The opening entry and opening balances
slides.body_md: At the start of the new books an **opening entry** debits every asset and credits every liability and the **capital**, which is the balancing figure. Each balance then opens its ledger account as **balance b/d**.

rows: *(Being the assets, the liability and the capital brought forward from the old books)*

visual.alt: Opening entry of Parvati Coir Works dated 1 April 2027: cash, stock and machinery debited, Venkat Fibre Co. and capital of four lakh sixty thousand rupees credited
visual.caption: Capital is the balancing figure of the opening entry

slides.narration: New books begin with an opening entry. Every asset is debited. Every liability is credited. Capital is the difference between the assets and the liabilities, so it is credited with the balancing figure. When the opening entry is posted, each account starts with its old balance, shown as balance brought down, on the debit side for an asset and on the credit side for a liability or capital.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: posting simple entries to the cash account
slides.body_md: **Parvati Coir Works**, an imagined firm in Kerala, starts on 1 April 2027 with cash ₹85,000. It sells goods for cash for ₹3,10,000 on 9 April and pays ₹2,50,000 to Venkat Fibre Co. on 15 May. Post these to the Cash A/c.
bullets: The opening balance is a debit: **To Balance b/d**.
The cash sale is a debit; the other account is **Sales**.
The payment is a credit; the other account is **Venkat Fibre Co.**.

rows: 15 May By Venkat Fibre Co. A/c (J.F. 1)

visual.alt: Cash A/c of Parvati Coir Works after posting three entries: the opening balance of eighty five thousand rupees and a cash sale on the debit side, a payment to Venkat Fibre Co. on the credit side
visual.caption: Posted, not yet balanced

slides.narration: The cash account opens with the balance brought down, rupees eighty five thousand, on the debit side. The cash sale of rupees three lakh ten thousand is a debit, written To Sales. The payment of rupees two lakh fifty thousand to the supplier is a credit, written By Venkat Fibre Co. Cash is not balanced yet, because the period is still running.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a posting
slides.body_md: Apply the rule of posting to an expense paid in cash.
slides.narration: Decide which account is debited, then recall which word is written on that side and which account is named.

slides.heading: Compound entries and Sundries
slides.body_md: A **compound entry** has more than two accounts. Each account is still posted on its own side, and the account whose side has several accounts opposite it shows **Sundries**.

rows: *(Being wages and rent paid in cash)*
*(Being furniture bought, part paid in cash and the rest owed to Venkat Fibre Co.)*

visual.alt: Two compound journal entries of Parvati Coir Works: wages and rent paid together in cash, and furniture bought partly for cash and partly on credit from Venkat Fibre Co.
visual.caption: Each compound entry is posted to every account it names

slides.narration: The wages and rent entry debits two accounts and credits cash once. Wages and rent each show To Cash, but cash shows By Sundries for the total of rupees seventy eight thousand. The furniture entry credits two accounts, so furniture shows To Sundries, while cash and the supplier each show By Furniture.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a supplier's account before balancing
slides.body_md: Venkat Fibre Co. is owed ₹65,000 on 1 April 2027. The firm buys goods on credit for ₹2,40,000, pays ₹2,50,000, buys furniture partly on credit and returns goods worth ₹15,000. Post to the account.
bullets: The opening balance of a creditor is on the **credit** side.
Payments and returns are on the **debit** side.
Credit purchases and the credit part of the furniture are on the **credit** side.

visual.alt: Account of Venkat Fibre Co. in the ledger of Parvati Coir Works before balancing: the opening balance, a credit purchase and the balance of the furniture on the credit side, a payment and a return on the debit side
visual.caption: Personal account: posted, not yet balanced

slides.narration: The supplier is owed rupees sixty five thousand at the start, so the account opens on the credit side. Goods bought on credit are credited. The payment of rupees two lakh fifty thousand and the goods returned are debits, because they reduce what the firm owes. The furniture bought on credit adds the unpaid part to the credit side.

slides.heading: Quick check: the two folios
slides.body_md: Which folio goes in which book?
slides.narration: Recall where each folio is written and what it points to.

slides.heading: Balancing a real or personal account
slides.body_md: At the end of the period, real and personal accounts are **balanced**. The balance is carried to the next period.

nodes.label: Write it on the smaller side as balance c/d
Write the equal total on both sides
Bring it down below as balance b/d

visual.alt: Five steps of balancing a ledger account: total each side, find the difference, write it as balance carried down on the smaller side, write the equal total on both sides and bring the balance down on the opposite side
visual.caption: Balancing a real or personal account

slides.narration: To balance an account, total each side, then find the difference. Write the difference on the smaller side as balance carried down, so that both sides total the same. Write that total on both sides on the same line. Then bring the balance down below the totals on the opposite side as balance brought down, which opens the next period.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: balancing the cash account
slides.body_md: Balance the Cash A/c of Parvati Coir Works for the year ended 31 March 2028. The debit side is the opening cash, the cash sales, the sum received from Ismail and Sons and the interest; the credit side holds every payment.
bullets: Debit side total before balancing is larger, so there is a **debit balance** of ₹1,25,000.
It is written **By Balance c/d** on the smaller side and brought down as **To Balance b/d** on 1 April 2028.

rows: 15 May By Venkat Fibre Co. A/c (J.F. 1)
12 Aug To Ismail and Sons A/c (J.F. 1)

visual.alt: Cash A/c of Parvati Coir Works balanced on 31 March 2028: both sides total the same, with a balance carried down on the credit side and brought down on the debit side as one lakh twenty five thousand rupees
visual.caption: Debit balance of cash carried down and brought down

slides.narration: After all postings the debit side is larger. The difference of rupees one lakh twenty five thousand is written on the credit side as balance carried down. Both sides then total rupees five lakh twenty seven thousand. On the first of April the balance is brought down on the debit side, so cash in hand is rupees one lakh twenty five thousand.

slides.heading: Reading debit and credit balances
slides.body_md: A balance carried down is either **debit** or **credit**. It tells what the account now means.

rows: Amount to be received from the customer
Amount still to be paid to the supplier
Amount owed by the firm to the proprietor

visual.alt: Table reading the closing balances of Parvati Coir Works: cash and the customer have debit balances and are assets, the supplier and the capital have credit balances

slides.narration: A debit balance means the account has more debits than credits. For cash and other assets it is the value in hand, and for a customer it is what he still owes. A credit balance means more credits. For a supplier it is the amount the firm owes, and for capital it is the amount owed to the proprietor. So balances are read by their side and the nature of the account.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: balancing a creditor and reading the balance
slides.body_md: Balance the account of Venkat Fibre Co. on 31 March 2028. The credit side is larger, so the balance is **credit**. The account of Ismail and Sons, a customer, closes with a **debit** balance of ₹50,000.

visual.alt: Account of Venkat Fibre Co. balanced on 31 March 2028: a credit balance of eighty five thousand rupees is carried down on the debit side and brought down on the credit side
visual.caption: Credit balance of a supplier

slides.narration: The credit side of the supplier is larger, so the balance of rupees eighty five thousand is written on the debit side as balance carried down and brought down on the credit side. It is a liability. The customer Ismail and Sons, in contrast, has a debit balance of rupees fifty thousand, an asset to be received.

slides.heading: Quick check: finding a balance
slides.body_md: Total each side separately before you subtract.
slides.narration: Add the debits, add the credits and take the difference. The larger side tells you the nature of the balance.

slides.heading: Slips to avoid

rows: Naming the account itself in its own account
The account is already the heading of the page
Name the other account of the entry
Writing To on the credit side
To belongs to the debit side
To on the debit side, By on the credit side
Writing the balance c/d on the larger side
Put it on the smaller side
An expense or income of one year has no use next year
The old balance is part of the account
Bring it in as balance b/d first

visual.alt: Table of five common slips when posting and balancing ledger accounts, why each is wrong and the correct practice

slides.narration: Five slips cost marks. Do not name the account itself in its own page. Do not write To on the credit side. Do not put the balance on the larger side. Do not carry down a nominal account, which is closed instead. And do not forget to bring in the opening balance. Check the sides, the other account named and the equal totals every time.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Principal book; one account for each head; written up from the journal
Debit side: To the other account. Credit side: By the other account. Sundries for several
L.F. in the journal; J.F. in the ledger; both filled after posting
Opening entry; each balance comes in as b/d on its own side
Difference on the smaller side as c/d; equal totals; b/d on the opposite side below
Debit balance: asset or amount due from a person. Credit balance: liability or capital

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the ledger, the rule of posting, folios, opening balances, balancing and reading balances

slides.narration: To sum up. The ledger is the principal book, written up from the journal with an account for each head. Each debit is posted with To and the other account, and each credit with By. The folios link the two books. Real and personal accounts are balanced with a balance carried down and brought down, and the side of the balance shows its nature.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Bring in every **opening balance** first, on its correct side.
Name the **other account** with **To** or **By**; use **Sundries** for compound entries.
Write the balance on the **smaller** side as **balance c/d**; bring it down as **b/d** below the totals.
State whether the closing balance is a **debit** or a **credit**.
Show the **equal totals**: they usually carry step marks.
slides.narration: Examiners give marks for the opening balances, for correct particulars, for the balance and for the totals. Common slips are naming the account in itself, writing the amount on the wrong side, forgetting the opening balance and putting the balance on the larger side. Always check that the two totals are equal before moving on.

decks.title: Ledger — Part 2: Closing Nominal Accounts, Closing and Adjusting Entries
goals: Explain why nominal accounts are closed by transfer to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account and not carried down
Pass closing entries for purchases, sales, returns, opening stock, direct and indirect expenses and incomes, and for profit and drawings
Pass simple adjusting entries for closing stock, outstanding and prepaid expenses, accrued and advance income and depreciation

slides.heading: Closing and adjusting entries
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how **nominal accounts** are closed, the **closing entries** for the Trading and Profit and Loss Accounts, and **adjusting entries** at an introductory level.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: adjusting entries bring accruals into the books, closing entries move the nominal accounts to the Trading and Profit and Loss Accounts and the profit goes to the Capital Account
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part two we finish the year. Expenses and incomes of the year cannot be carried to the next year, so they are transferred to the Trading Account and the Profit and Loss Account by closing entries. Before that, adjusting entries bring in the items that belong to the year but are not yet recorded. We use the same coir works, with a second firm for adjustments.

slides.heading: Nominal accounts are closed, not carried down
slides.body_md: Real and personal accounts are **balanced** and carried down. **Nominal accounts** record the expenses and incomes of one period, so they are **closed by transfer** and show no balance c/d.

rows: Purchases, sales, wages, rent, interest received
Expenses, losses, incomes and gains of one period
At the end of the period
Balanced: balance c/d, then balance b/d
Closed by transfer to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account

visual.alt: Table contrasting real and personal accounts, which are balanced and carried down, with nominal accounts, which are closed by transfer and open empty in the next period

slides.narration: Cash, machinery, debtors and creditors still matter next year, so they are balanced and carried down. Purchases, sales, wages and rent belong to the year just ended. At the year end they are closed by transfer to the Trading Account or the Profit and Loss Account. They have no balance carried down and open the new year empty.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: closing the wages account
slides.body_md: Wages paid in cash by Parvati Coir Works were ₹48,000, and ₹4,000 of wages is due at the year end. The adjusting entry brings in the amount due, and the whole expense is then transferred to the Trading Account.
bullets: The wages account is closed by a **credit** of its total.
Its two sides then agree; there is **no balance c/d**.

visual.alt: Wages A/c of Parvati Coir Works: wages paid in cash, wages due added by the adjusting entry, and the full amount transferred to the Trading Account so that the account has no balance
visual.caption: A nominal account closes with no balance

slides.narration: Wages of rupees forty eight thousand were paid, and rupees four thousand more is due, so the expense for the year is rupees fifty two thousand. Wages is a direct expense, so it is credited with the full amount, written By Trading Account. Both sides total the same, and nothing is carried down. The next year starts with no wages balance.

slides.heading: Closing entries: what goes where
slides.body_md: A **closing entry** is a journal entry passed at the end of the period to transfer a nominal account to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account. One entry is passed for each account.

rows: Trading A/c Dr, to the account
Trading A/c Dr, to the account
The account Dr, to Trading A/c
Closing Stock A/c Dr, to Trading A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr, to the account
The account Dr, to Profit and Loss A/c

visual.alt: Table showing where each nominal account is closed: stock, purchases, sales returns and direct expenses are debited to the Trading Account; sales, purchases returns and closing stock are credited to it; indirect expenses are debited and incomes credited to the Profit and Loss Account

slides.narration: Sort the nominal accounts first. Items that make up the cost of goods go to the Trading Account: opening stock, purchases, sales returns, direct expenses such as wages and carriage inwards, and on the credit side sales, purchases returns and closing stock. Indirect expenses and incomes go to the Profit and Loss Account. A debit balance is cleared by a credit, a credit balance by a debit.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: closing the trading items
slides.body_md: Parvati Coir Works closes opening stock (held in Stock A/c), purchases, sales return, sales and purchases return on 31 March 2028. Accounts with a debit balance are **credited**, accounts with a credit balance are **debited**.

rows: *(Being Sales Return transferred to Trading Account)*
*(Being Purchases Return transferred to Trading Account)*

visual.alt: Closing entries of Parvati Coir Works for opening stock, purchases, sales return, sales and purchases return, each carrying the date 31 March 2028 and a narration
visual.caption: Closing journal entries for the trading items

slides.narration: For opening stock, purchases and sales return, the Trading Account is debited and the account itself is credited, which clears its debit balance. For sales and purchases return the account is debited, which clears its credit balance, and the Trading Account is credited. Each entry carries its own narration.

slides.heading: Quick check: which account is closed by transfer?
slides.body_md: Decide first whether the account is nominal.
slides.narration: Nominal accounts are closed by transfer. Then think of whether the item is a direct expense or an indirect one.

slides.heading: Expenses and incomes to Trading and Profit and Loss
slides.body_md: Direct expenses, wages and carriage inwards, go to the **Trading Account**. Indirect expenses such as rent and depreciation, and incomes such as interest received, go to the **Profit and Loss Account**.

rows: *(Being Carriage Inwards transferred to Trading Account)*
*(Being Rent transferred to Profit and Loss Account)*
*(Being Depreciation transferred to Profit and Loss Account)*
*(Being Interest Received transferred to Profit and Loss Account)*

visual.alt: Closing entries for wages and carriage inwards, which go to the Trading Account, and for rent, depreciation and interest received, which go to the Profit and Loss Account
visual.caption: Direct and indirect expenses and incomes

slides.narration: Wages and carriage inwards are direct expenses, so they are credited and the Trading Account is debited. Rent and depreciation are indirect expenses, so the Profit and Loss Account is debited and the expense is credited. Interest received is an income, so it is debited and the Profit and Loss Account is credited. The rent here is the amount for the year, after the prepaid part.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the Trading Account after closing
slides.body_md: After every closing entry is posted, the **Trading Account** shows the cost items on the debit side and sales, purchases return and closing stock on the credit side. The difference is the **gross profit**, ₹1,65,000, transferred to the Profit and Loss Account.

rows: 31 Mar 2028 To Profit and Loss A/c (J.F. 2)

visual.alt: Trading Account of Parvati Coir Works in ledger form after the closing entries: opening stock, purchases, sales return, wages and carriage inwards on the debit side, sales, purchases return and closing stock on the credit side, and a gross profit of one lakh sixty five thousand rupees transferred
visual.caption: Trading A/c after the closing entries

slides.narration: The debit side holds opening stock, purchases, sales return, wages and carriage. The credit side holds sales, purchases return and closing stock. The credit side is larger, and the difference of rupees one lakh sixty five thousand is the gross profit, passed on to the Profit and Loss Account. Both sides total rupees six lakh fifteen thousand, so the Trading Account is closed.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 (contd): the Profit and Loss Account
slides.body_md: Rent and depreciation are debited and interest received and the gross profit are credited. The difference is the **net profit**, ₹1,25,000, transferred to the Capital Account.

visual.alt: Profit and Loss Account of Parvati Coir Works after the closing entries: rent and depreciation on the debit side, gross profit and interest received on the credit side, and a net profit of one lakh twenty five thousand rupees transferred to capital
visual.caption: Profit and Loss A/c after the closing entries

slides.narration: The Profit and Loss Account has rent and depreciation on the debit side, and the gross profit with interest received on the credit side. The credit side is larger by rupees one lakh twenty five thousand. This net profit is debited here and credited to the Capital Account. Both sides total rupees one lakh eighty thousand, so this account is closed as well.

slides.heading: Profit and drawings go to capital
slides.body_md: The **gross profit** moves from Trading to Profit and Loss; the **net profit** moves to the **Capital Account**; **drawings** are also transferred to the Capital Account.

rows: *(Being gross profit transferred to Profit and Loss Account)*
*(Being net profit transferred to Capital Account)*

visual.alt: Closing entries for the gross profit, the net profit and the drawings of Parvati Coir Works, ending with the transfer to the Capital Account
visual.caption: Profit and drawings move to capital

slides.narration: Three more closing entries finish the job. The Trading Account is debited and the Profit and Loss Account credited with the gross profit. The Profit and Loss Account is debited and the Capital Account credited with the net profit. And the Capital Account is debited with the drawings, which are credited. A loss would reverse the first two.

slides.heading: The capital account after closing
bullets: Net profit **adds** to capital; drawings **reduce** it.
Capital is a personal-type account: it is **balanced** and carried down.

rows: 31 Mar 2028 By Profit and Loss A/c (J.F. 2)

visual.alt: Capital A/c of Parvati Coir Works after the closing entries: opening capital and net profit on the credit side, drawings on the debit side, and a closing balance of five lakh forty nine thousand rupees carried down and brought down
visual.caption: Capital A/c at the end of the year

slides.narration: Capital opens with rupees four lakh sixty thousand. The net profit is credited and the drawings are debited. What remains, rupees five lakh forty nine thousand, is carried down and brought down. Notice that capital, unlike the nominal accounts, is balanced, not closed by transfer.

slides.heading: Quick check: a closing entry
slides.body_md: Think of what a nominal account looks like after the entry.
slides.narration: Decide whether closing entries clear nominal accounts and where the balance is sent.

slides.heading: Adjusting entries: meaning and purpose
slides.body_md: An **adjusting entry** is passed at the end of the period to record an item that belongs to the period but is not yet in the books, or one that belongs to the next period. Full final accounts come in Chapters 12 and 13.

headers: Charged or credited for the year (₹)

visual.alt: Table of four adjustments in the books of Hosur Candle Works: salaries due are added, insurance paid in advance is deducted, commission earned but not received is added and rent received in advance is deducted, each with the asset or liability that results
visual.caption: Hosur Candle Works, an imagined firm: year ended 31 March 2028

slides.narration: Adjusting entries correct the figures of the year. An expense not yet paid must be added, an expense paid ahead for the next year must be taken out, income earned but not received must be added, and income received for the next year must be taken out. Only then is the profit of the year true and the balance sheet complete.

slides.heading: Closing stock
slides.body_md: Stock left at the end of the year is brought into the books by debiting **Closing Stock A/c** and crediting the **Trading Account**.

rows: *(Being closing stock brought into the Trading Account)*

visual.alt: Entry bringing the closing stock of sixty four thousand rupees into the books, with the two places where it appears: the credit side of the Trading Account and the assets in the balance sheet
visual.caption: Closing stock entry

slides.narration: If the closing stock is valued at rupees sixty four thousand, the closing stock account is debited and the Trading Account credited. In the Trading Account it appears on the credit side, because it reduces the cost of goods sold. In the balance sheet it is a current asset, and the balance is brought down as the next period's opening stock.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: adjusting entries for expenses and incomes
slides.body_md: **Hosur Candle Works**, an imagined firm, has salaries of ₹7,000 due, insurance of ₹2,400 paid in advance, commission of ₹5,000 earned but not received and rent of ₹9,000 received in advance. Pass the entries.

rows: *(Being insurance paid for the next year)*
*(Being commission earned but not yet received)*
To Rent Received in Advance A/c
*(Being rent received for the next year)*

visual.alt: Four adjusting entries of Hosur Candle Works: outstanding salaries, prepaid insurance, accrued commission and rent received in advance, each with its narration
visual.caption: Adjusting entries at 31 March 2028

slides.narration: Salaries due: debit salaries and credit outstanding salaries, a liability. Insurance paid ahead: debit prepaid insurance, an asset, and credit insurance. Commission earned but not received: debit accrued commission, an asset, and credit commission received. Rent received ahead: debit rent received and credit rent received in advance, a liability.

slides.heading: The rule behind each adjusting entry
bullets: **Outstanding** and **advance** items are **liabilities**.
**Prepaid** and **accrued** items are **assets**.

rows: Expense A/c Dr to Outstanding Expense A/c

sections.heading: 1. The ledger: meaning, importance and format
sections.body_md:
**Ledger:** the principal book of accounts in which every transaction recorded in the journal is classified under separate heads, each head having an account of its own. It is a book of secondary entry, because it is written up from the journal.

**Importance:** all transactions of one account are brought together; the balance of each account (cash in hand, amount due from a customer, amount owed to a supplier) is easily found; it supplies the figures for the trial balance and the final accounts.

**Format (T-form):** a two-sided account. The left side is the **debit** side, the right side the **credit** side; each side has columns for date, particulars, journal folio and amount, and the debit side particulars begin with **To** and the credit side particulars with **By**.

**Running balance form (mention):** columns for date, particulars, folio, debit, credit and a balance recomputed after every entry; useful for customer and supplier accounts.

sections.heading: 2. Folios and the rule of posting
sections.body_md:
**Posting** is the process of copying journal entries to the ledger accounts.

- **Debit** of the entry: the account is written on its debit side, with **To** and the name of the other account.
- **Credit** of the entry: the account is written on its credit side, with **By** and the name of the other account.
- **Several accounts** on the other side: write **Sundries**.
- An account never names itself.

**Ledger folio (L.F.):** page of the account in the ledger; written in the journal after the entry is posted. **Journal folio (J.F.):** page of the journal; written in the ledger beside each posted item.

sections.body_md:
When a new set of books begins, an **opening entry** is passed: every asset is debited and every liability and the capital are credited. **Capital** = assets − liabilities.

Posting the opening entry opens each ledger account with its balance, written as **To Balance b/d** on the debit side for an asset, or **By Balance b/d** on the credit side for a liability or capital. Later transactions are posted below these opening balances.

sections.heading: 4. Balancing real and personal accounts
sections.body_md:
Real accounts (cash, machinery, stock held) and personal accounts (debtors, creditors, capital) are **balanced** at the end of the period.

1. Total each side.
2. Take the difference of the two totals.
3. Enter the difference on the **smaller** side as **Balance c/d**.
4. Write the equal total on both sides on one line.
5. Bring the balance down on the opposite side, below the totals, as **Balance b/d**.

A larger debit side gives a **debit** balance, shown By Balance c/d on the credit side. A larger credit side gives a **credit** balance, shown To Balance c/d on the debit side.

sections.heading: 6. Closing nominal accounts: closing entries
sections.body_md:
**Nominal accounts** (expenses, losses, incomes, gains) are not carried down. They are **closed by transfer** to the Trading Account or the Profit and Loss Account at the end of the period, through **closing entries**: one entry for each account, with a narration.

- **Debit-balance** accounts are cleared by a **credit**: Trading A/c Dr to Opening Stock, Purchases, Sales Return, Wages and Carriage Inwards; Profit and Loss A/c Dr to indirect expenses.
- **Credit-balance** accounts are cleared by a **debit**: Sales, Purchases Return to Trading A/c; incomes to Profit and Loss A/c.
- **Closing stock** (after its adjusting entry) is a credit in the Trading Account.
- **Gross profit** (credit side of Trading larger) goes to Profit and Loss; a gross loss reverses the entry.
- **Net profit** goes to Capital A/c; a net loss reverses it; **drawings** are transferred to Capital A/c.

sections.heading: 7. Adjusting entries at introductory level
sections.body_md:
**Adjusting entries** are passed at the end of the period, before the closing entries, to bring in items that belong to the period but are not yet recorded, or to take out items that belong to the next period.

- **Closing stock:** Closing Stock A/c Dr to Trading A/c.
- **Outstanding expense:** Expense A/c Dr to Outstanding Expense A/c (liability).
- **Prepaid expense:** Prepaid Expense A/c Dr (asset) to Expense A/c.
- **Accrued income:** Accrued Income A/c Dr (asset) to Income A/c.
- **Income received in advance:** Income A/c Dr to Income Received in Advance A/c (liability).
- **Depreciation:** Depreciation A/c Dr to the asset account, then closed to the Profit and Loss Account.

Expense for the year = amount paid + outstanding − prepaid. Income for the year = amount received + accrued − received in advance. Complete final accounts and balance sheets with these items are treated in Chapters 12 and 13.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts, Section A)**
- 1 mark: one correct option, a term or the side of a balance.
- 2 marks: a short definition or distinction, one entry with narration or a simple balancing.
- 3 marks: a ledger account posted from a short journal and balanced, or a set of adjusting or closing entries.
- 5 marks: several accounts posted and balanced with their totals, or all the closing entries for a year, in proper form.

**Step marks** usually go for each correct account with its opening balance, the postings with the other account named, the balance c/d and b/d, and the equal totals.

**Common mistakes**
- Naming an account in its own page, or using By on the debit side.
- Leaving out an opening balance, or placing it on the wrong side.
- Writing the balance c/d on the larger side, or carrying down a nominal account.
- Crediting sales to close it, or putting closing stock on the debit side of the Trading Account.
- Treating an outstanding expense as an asset and a prepaid expense as a liability.
- Forgetting the narration under a journal entry.
